intro.title: A rebirth
intro.text: Italy, around 1400 to 1600. Artists revived the ideas of ancient Greece and Rome and put people, not just God, at the centre.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Deep, mathematically correct perspective. Calm, balanced groups. Real-looking bodies, studied from life.

intro.title: The big names
intro.text: Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael in Italy. Titian in Venice. In the north: van Eyck, Holbein, Bosch, Bruegel.

questions.q: 'Renaissance' means…
questions.explain: French for rebirth: the revival of classical learning and art.

questions.q: In which country did the Renaissance begin?
questions.explain: Florence in particular, funded by families like the Medici.

questions.q: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.explain: Leonardo, from about 1503. It's in the Louvre.

questions.q: Who painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling?
questions.explain: Michelangelo, 1508–12. He saw himself as a sculptor first.

questions.q: What did Renaissance painters use to make space look deep and real?
questions.explain: Lines converging on a vanishing point. Brunelleschi worked it out in Florence in the early 1400s.

questions.q: Leonardo's soft, smoky blending of edges is called…
questions.explain: From the Italian for smoke. Look at the corners of the Mona Lisa's mouth.

questions.q: Venice and Florence had different priorities. Venice prized…
questions.explain: Florence praised disegno (drawing); Venice, led by Titian, praised colore.

questions.q: What's hidden across the floor of Holbein's The Ambassadors?
questions.explain: An anamorphic skull: view it from the side and it snaps into shape. A reminder of death.

questions.q: Where can you see The Birth of Venus?
questions.explain: In the Uffizi, along with Botticelli's Primavera.

questions.q: In The School of Athens, who is said to have Leonardo's face?
questions.explain: Plato, pointing upwards, at the centre.

questions.q: Bruegel's Hunters in the Snow belongs to a series showing…
questions.explain: A set of seasonal scenes. Five survive; three are in Vienna.

intro.title: In the news
intro.text: 'Van Eyck: The Portraits' at the National Gallery, 21 November 2026 to 11 April 2027, gathers his surviving portraits together for the first time.

intro.title: Who was he?
intro.text: A Flemish painter working in Bruges, court painter to the Duke of Burgundy. One of the founders of 'Northern Renaissance' art.

intro.title: Oil magic
intro.text: He perfected oil glazes: thin transparent layers that make fur, metal, skin and light glow. Look at every reflection.

questions.q: Where did Jan van Eyck work?
questions.explain: Bruges, in today's Belgium, the great trading city of the 1400s.

questions.q: Which of his paintings hangs in the National Gallery, London?
questions.explain: Bought in 1842. It's the centrepiece of the new show.

questions.q: Van Eyck is famous for mastering which material?
questions.explain: He didn't invent oil paint, but he took it further than anyone before him.

questions.q: What's the hallmark of a van Eyck painting?
questions.explain: You can count the hairs in the fur and see windows reflected in the mirror.

questions.q: Van Eyck's motto, painted on frames, was…
questions.explain: A pun on his name: 'As I/Eyck can'.

questions.q: What's on the back wall of the Arnolfini Portrait?
options: A convex mirror reflecting two more people
questions.explain: Above it he wrote, in Latin: 'Jan van Eyck was here 1434'.

questions.q: Which great altarpiece did he complete in 1432?
questions.explain: Begun with his brother Hubert, in St Bavo's Cathedral, Ghent.

questions.q: The man in the red turban (National Gallery) may be…
questions.explain: Many think it's a self-portrait; the frame carries his motto.

intro.title: Drama
intro.text: The 1600s wanted art you feel in your stomach: diagonal movement, big emotion, a frozen moment of action.

intro.title: Light out of darkness
intro.text: Caravaggio lit figures like a spotlight in a dark room. The style spread across Europe.

intro.title: The Dutch Golden Age
intro.text: Protestant Holland went quieter: portraits, interiors, still lifes. Rembrandt in Amsterdam, Vermeer in Delft.

questions.q: Roughly when was the Baroque period?
questions.explain: From about 1600 to 1750.

questions.q: Who painted The Night Watch?
questions.explain: Rembrandt, 1642. It's in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam.

questions.q: Who painted Girl with a Pearl Earring?
questions.explain: Vermeer, about 1665. It's in the Mauritshuis, The Hague.

questions.q: What's the strongest visual sign of Baroque painting?
questions.explain: Chiaroscuro: strong contrast of light and dark.

questions.q: Caravaggio's extreme light-and-dark is called…
questions.explain: From the Italian tenebroso, murky.

questions.q: Vermeer's interiors are usually lit from…
questions.explain: Soft daylight from the left falls across a quiet room.

questions.q: Who appears in the mirror at the back of Las Meninas?
options: The king and queen of Spain
questions.explain: Philip IV and Queen Mariana. Velázquez himself stands at the easel.

questions.q: Where can you see Rembrandt's Self-Portrait with Two Circles for free?
questions.explain: At Kenwood on Hampstead Heath.

questions.q: Artemisia Gentileschi was the first woman admitted to…
questions.explain: In 1616. Her Judith paintings are among the most powerful of the age.

questions.q: Which London painting did a suffragette slash in 1914?
questions.explain: Mary Richardson attacked Velázquez's Venus in the National Gallery. It was repaired.

intro.title: Light and playful
intro.text: After Baroque grandeur, 18th-century France went pastel: flirting aristocrats, swings, dreamy gardens.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Soft pinks and blues, curling decoration, feathery brushwork, pleasure and leisure.

intro.title: Key names
intro.text: Watteau, Boucher and Fragonard. And in London, the Wallace Collection has one of the world's best Rococo collections, free.

questions.q: Rococo flourished mainly in which country?
questions.explain: Paris and the court of Louis XV.

questions.q: Which London museum holds Fragonard's The Swing?
questions.explain: The Wallace Collection, Manchester Square. Free to visit.

questions.q: Which colours feel most Rococo?
questions.explain: Light, sweet and decorative.

questions.q: Rococo paintings are usually about…
questions.explain: Pleasure for an aristocratic audience.

questions.q: The 'fête galante' (elegant outdoor party) was invented for…
questions.explain: The French Academy created the category in 1717 for his Pilgrimage to Cythera.

questions.q: Boucher's most famous patron was…
questions.explain: Louis XV's favourite. The Toilet of Venus was painted for her.

intro.title: Britain finds its voice
intro.text: In the 1700s British art stepped out from foreign painters: satire, society portraits, horses and science.

intro.title: Hogarth and Gainsborough
intro.text: Hogarth told moral stories in picture series. Gainsborough painted elegant portraits set in landscape.

intro.title: Stubbs and Wright
intro.text: Stubbs painted horses with an anatomist's eye. Joseph Wright of Derby painted science by candlelight.

questions.q: Which institution was founded in London in 1768?
questions.explain: With Joshua Reynolds as its first President.

questions.q: George Stubbs is best known for painting…
questions.explain: He dissected horses to publish The Anatomy of the Horse (1766).

questions.q: Hogarth's 'modern moral subjects' tell a story across…
questions.explain: Like A Rake's Progress or Marriage A-la-Mode, sold as cheap prints too.

questions.q: Gainsborough's portraits often place sitters…
options: In front of a black background
questions.explain: He loved landscape and painted it with feathery brushwork.

questions.q: What's unfinished in Mr and Mrs Andrews?
questions.explain: An empty patch where something, maybe a bird or a child, was planned.

questions.q: Hogarth's pug was called…
questions.explain: It appears in his self-portrait, The Painter and his Pug.

questions.q: What light source does Wright of Derby use in the Air Pump painting?
questions.explain: Candlelight makes science look like a sacred drama.

intro.title: Feeling first
intro.text: A reaction to the Age of Reason: emotion, imagination and the wild power of nature.

intro.title: The sublime
intro.text: Beauty mixed with terror. Storms, mountains and shipwrecks, with tiny humans to show the scale.

intro.title: Key names
intro.text: Turner and Constable in Britain, Friedrich in Germany, Delacroix and Géricault in France, Goya in Spain.

questions.q: Roughly when was Romanticism?
questions.explain: Around the turn of the 19th century.

questions.q: Romantic artists valued above all…
questions.explain: Feeling over reason.

questions.q: Which two British painters are the giants of Romantic landscape?
questions.explain: Turner for drama and light, Constable for the English countryside.

questions.q: The 'sublime' means…
questions.explain: Nature as overwhelming and dangerous.

questions.q: Turner's late style is known for…
options: Swirling light and colour that dissolve shapes
questions.explain: Critics called some of his late pictures 'soapsuds and whitewash'.

questions.q: The Hay Wain was painted by…
questions.explain: In 1821, near Flatford in Suffolk. It's in the National Gallery.

questions.q: What does The Fighting Temeraire show?
options: A warship towed to be broken up
questions.explain: A Trafalgar veteran pulled by a steam tug: the old age giving way to the new.

questions.q: What tiny animal runs ahead of the train in Rain, Steam and Speed?
questions.explain: Can nature outrun the machine?

questions.q: Liberty Leading the People celebrates the revolution of…
questions.explain: The July Revolution. Delacroix painted it the same year.

questions.q: The Raft of the Medusa was based on…
questions.explain: Géricault interviewed survivors and studied corpses.

intro.title: A secret brotherhood
intro.text: Founded in London in 1848 by three young students: Dante Gabriel Rossetti, John Everett Millais and William Holman Hunt.

intro.title: Why the name?
intro.text: They rejected the art schools' worship of Raphael and looked to the bright, detailed art before him.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Jewel-bright colour, every leaf painted, stories from Shakespeare, Tennyson and legend. Tate Britain holds the key works.

questions.q: The Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood was founded in…
questions.explain: 1848, a year of revolutions across Europe.

questions.q: Where in London are the great Pre-Raphaelite paintings?
questions.explain: Ophelia, The Lady of Shalott, Proserpine and more.

questions.q: Which was NOT a founding member?
questions.explain: Waterhouse came a generation later, borrowing their style.

questions.q: Pre-Raphaelite paintings are known for…
questions.explain: They painted on a wet white ground to make colours glow.

questions.q: Their stories mostly came from…
questions.explain: Shakespeare, Tennyson, Dante, Arthurian legend.

questions.q: Who modelled for Millais' Ophelia?
questions.explain: She lay in a bath of water for hours and caught a bad cold.

questions.q: In Proserpine, what does the pomegranate mean?
options: She must stay in the underworld
questions.explain: Eating its seeds bound her to Hades. The model is Jane Morris.

questions.q: The Lady of Shalott comes from a poem by…
questions.explain: Waterhouse painted it in 1888.

intro.title: Paint what you see
intro.text: In 1840s France, artists turned from heroes and myths to ordinary people: workers, peasants, funerals.

intro.title: Courbet
intro.text: Gustave Courbet led the charge: 'Show me an angel and I'll paint one.'

intro.title: Manet's scandals
intro.text: Manet took old-master poses and filled them with modern Parisians. Critics were outraged.

questions.q: Realism began in which country?
questions.explain: Around 1848, with Courbet and Millet.

questions.q: Realists chose to paint…
questions.explain: Everyday life at the size usually kept for history paintings.

questions.q: Why did The Gleaners upset critics?
options: It showed poverty at heroic scale
questions.explain: Poor women gathering leftover grain looked like a political statement.

questions.q: Which painting shows a modern courtesan in a classic Venus pose?
questions.explain: Manet, 1863, after Titian's Venus of Urbino.

questions.q: Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe was shown at the…
questions.explain: The 1863 show of works the official Salon rejected.

questions.q: What happened to Courbet's The Stone Breakers?
questions.explain: Destroyed in the Second World War near Dresden.

intro.title: Light, right now
intro.text: Catching a fleeting moment: sunlight on water, a breezy afternoon, a busy boulevard. Often painted outdoors.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Quick visible brushstrokes, bright unmixed colour, coloured shadows, everyday modern life.

intro.title: A rude name
intro.text: A critic mocked Monet's Impression, Sunrise at the group's first show in Paris in 1874. The insult stuck.

questions.q: The first Impressionist exhibition was held in Paris in…
questions.explain: In the former studio of the photographer Nadar.

questions.q: The movement is named after a painting by…
questions.explain: Impression, Sunrise (1872).

questions.q: Painting 'en plein air' means painting…
questions.explain: New paint tubes made it practical.

questions.q: Which Impressionist was American?
questions.explain: Cassatt, from Pittsburgh, exhibited with the group.

questions.q: Which is most typical of Impressionism?
questions.explain: The brushwork shows: it captures movement and light.

questions.q: How did Impressionists paint shadows?
options: With colour, often blue or violet
questions.explain: Shadows contain colour from the sky and surroundings.

questions.q: Bal du moulin de la Galette shows…
questions.explain: Renoir, 1876, dappled light through trees.

questions.q: Which Manet painting hangs in the Courtauld Gallery, London?
questions.explain: His last major painting, 1882.

questions.q: Gustave Caillebotte also helped the group by…
questions.explain: A wealthy painter, he bought and funded his friends' work.

questions.q: Berthe Morisot exhibited in how many of the eight Impressionist shows?
questions.explain: All but 1879, when she'd just had a daughter.

intro.title: Beyond the moment
intro.text: Artists who started from Impressionism but wanted more: structure, emotion, symbolism.

intro.title: Four routes
intro.text: Cézanne built form from blocks of colour. Van Gogh poured out feeling. Gauguin chased the symbolic. Seurat painted in dots.

intro.title: Named in London
intro.text: The critic Roger Fry coined the term for his 1910 London show. Visitors were outraged.

questions.q: Who coined the term 'Post-Impressionism'?
questions.explain: For 'Manet and the Post-Impressionists' at the Grafton Galleries, London, 1910.

questions.q: Which painter is NOT a Post-Impressionist?
questions.explain: Monet stayed an Impressionist to the end.

questions.q: The Starry Night was painted by…
questions.explain: In 1889, at the asylum in Saint-Rémy. It's at MoMA.

questions.q: Painting with tiny dots of pure colour is called…
questions.explain: Seurat's method, mixed by your eye at a distance.

questions.q: Van Gogh's brushwork is best described as…
questions.explain: He laid paint on thickly, often straight from the tube.

questions.q: Cézanne built his pictures from…
options: Blocks of colour and simple shapes
questions.explain: He said he wanted to treat nature through the cylinder, sphere and cone.

questions.q: Which version of Sunflowers can you see in London?
questions.explain: Painted in Arles in 1888 to decorate Gauguin's room.

questions.q: Gauguin painted Where Do We Come From? in…
questions.explain: In 1897. It reads right to left, from birth to old age.

questions.q: Which Seurat painting is in the National Gallery, London?
options: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
questions.explain: Workers relaxing by the Seine, 1884.

questions.q: Who appears in the background of At the Moulin Rouge?
questions.explain: The short man in the bowler hat.

intro.title: The floating world
intro.text: Ukiyo-e: 'pictures of the floating world'. Actors, beauties, landscapes, sold as cheap woodblock prints.

intro.title: How prints worked
intro.text: A designer drew, a carver cut one block per colour, a printer pressed them in turn. Many copies, so many museums own one.

intro.title: They changed Western art
intro.text: When the prints reached Europe, Monet, Van Gogh and Degas collected them. Flat colour and bold cropping followed.

questions.q: Ukiyo-e means…
questions.explain: A Buddhist idea of fleeting life, recast as city pleasures.

questions.q: Who made The Great Wave?
questions.explain: About 1831.

questions.q: How were ukiyo-e made?
questions.explain: One carved block for each colour.

questions.q: What did European artists borrow from Japanese prints?
questions.explain: Called Japonisme. Look at Cassatt and Van Gogh.

questions.q: The Great Wave comes from which series?
options: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
questions.explain: Hokusai, c.1830–32. Red Fuji is from it too.

questions.q: Which Hiroshige print did Van Gogh copy in oil?
questions.explain: In 1887, along with the Sudden Shower.

intro.title: The Secession
intro.text: In 1897 Klimt and friends broke away from Vienna's official art body to found the Vienna Secession.

intro.title: Gold
intro.text: Klimt's 'golden period' used real gold leaf and patterns from mosaics and decorative art.

intro.title: Record breaker
intro.text: In November 2025 his Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer sold for $236.4m, a record for modern art at auction.

questions.q: The Vienna Secession was founded in…
questions.explain: Klimt was its first president.

questions.q: Where is Klimt's The Kiss?
questions.explain: In the Upper Belvedere since 1908.

questions.q: What makes The Kiss shimmer?
questions.explain: From Klimt's 'golden period'.

questions.q: Which Klimt set a record for modern art at auction in 2025?
questions.explain: $236.4m at Sotheby's New York.

questions.q: Which younger Viennese artist did Klimt mentor?
questions.explain: Schiele's twisted, raw figures took Klimt's line in a darker direction.

intro.title: Wild beasts
intro.text: At the 1905 Salon d'Automne in Paris, a critic called the painters 'fauves': wild beasts.

intro.title: Colour set free
intro.text: Green faces, red trees, orange skies. Colour expresses feeling, not reality.

intro.title: Who
intro.text: Henri Matisse led, with André Derain and Maurice de Vlaminck. Derain painted the Thames in blazing colour.

questions.q: 'Fauves' means…
questions.explain: The critic Louis Vauxcelles' jibe, 1905.

questions.q: Who led Fauvism?
questions.explain: Matisse; Braque also painted Fauvist works before Cubism.

questions.q: What's the defining feature of a Fauvist painting?
questions.explain: Colour as emotion.

questions.q: Woman with a Hat was shown at…
questions.explain: The show that named the movement.

questions.q: Matisse's Dance (1910) uses just three colours. Which?
questions.explain: Commissioned by the Moscow collector Sergei Shchukin.

intro.title: Inside out
intro.text: Painting how the world feels, not how it looks: anxiety, longing, energy.

intro.title: The forerunner
intro.text: Munch's The Scream (1893) came first. Van Gogh's emotional colour mattered too.

intro.title: Two German groups
intro.text: Die Brücke (Dresden, 1905, with Kirchner) and Der Blaue Reiter (Munich, 1911, with Kandinsky and Franz Marc).

questions.q: Expressionism is mainly linked with which country?
questions.explain: Dresden, Berlin and Munich.

questions.q: Who painted The Scream?
questions.explain: Norwegian, 1893. Several versions exist.

questions.q: Expressionist paintings aim to show…
questions.explain: Distortion and clashing colour express feeling.

questions.q: Which is typical of Expressionism?
questions.explain: Tension made visible.

questions.q: Die Brücke was founded in 1905 in…
questions.explain: By architecture students including Kirchner.

questions.q: Der Blaue Reiter was co-founded by Kandinsky and…
questions.explain: Munich, 1911. Marc loved blue horses.

questions.q: Where is the 1893 painted version of The Scream?
questions.explain: The National Museum in Oslo.

intro.title: Many views at once
intro.text: Picasso and Braque broke objects into facets, showing several sides at the same time.

intro.title: The shock
intro.text: Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) stunned even his friends. Cubism followed.

intro.title: Spreading out
intro.text: Léger's tubes, Picabia's colour, Duchamp's motion: Cubism became a language others bent.

questions.q: Who invented Cubism?
questions.explain: Working side by side in Paris from about 1908.

questions.q: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon is in…
questions.explain: Since 1939.

questions.q: The key idea of Cubism is…
questions.explain: Objects are broken into planes and reassembled.

questions.q: Early (Analytic) Cubist paintings mostly use…
questions.explain: A narrow palette so you focus on form.

questions.q: Gluing paper into a picture, used in Synthetic Cubism, is called…
questions.explain: Braque made the first one in 1912.

questions.q: Why was Léger's Cubism nicknamed 'Tubism'?
questions.explain: Look at Contrast of Forms.

questions.q: Nude Descending a Staircase caused a stir at which 1913 show?
questions.explain: One critic called it 'an explosion in a shingle factory'.

intro.title: No subject at all
intro.text: Around 1910 artists asked: can colour and shape alone carry meaning, like music?

intro.title: Three pioneers
intro.text: Kandinsky (musical and expressive), Malevich (pure geometry) and Mondrian (grids).

intro.title: De Stijl
intro.text: Mondrian's Dutch group, from 1917: only straight lines, black, white and the three primary colours.

questions.q: Abstract art shows…
questions.explain: Colour, line and shape for their own sake.

questions.q: Black Square (1915) was painted by…
questions.explain: In Petrograd, launching Suprematism.

questions.q: Mondrian's signature style uses…
options: Black grid lines and primary colours
questions.explain: Red, yellow, blue, with black and white.

questions.q: Kandinsky compared painting to…
questions.explain: He called big works 'Compositions' and 'Improvisations'.

questions.q: Malevich's movement of pure geometric shapes is called…
questions.explain: Launched in 1915.

questions.q: Broadway Boogie Woogie was inspired by…
questions.explain: Mondrian moved to New York in 1940.

questions.q: Mondrian's De Stijl group came from…
questions.explain: Founded 1917 with Theo van Doesburg.

intro.title: Anti-art
intro.text: Born in Zurich in 1916, at the Cabaret Voltaire, in disgust at the First World War. Nonsense as protest.

intro.title: Readymades
intro.text: Marcel Duchamp chose ordinary objects and declared them art. The idea mattered more than the making.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Collage, photomontage, chance, jokes, cut-up words.

questions.q: Dada began in 1916 in…
questions.explain: At the Cabaret Voltaire, founded by Hugo Ball and Emmy Hennings.

questions.q: Dada was a reaction to…
questions.explain: If reason led to war, Dada chose nonsense.

questions.q: A 'readymade' is…
options: An everyday object presented as art
questions.explain: Duchamp's invention.

questions.q: Duchamp's Fountain is a…
questions.explain: Signed 'R. Mutt', 1917. Tate's version is a 1964 replica.

questions.q: What did Duchamp add to the Mona Lisa in L.H.O.O.Q.?
questions.explain: On a cheap postcard, 1919.

intro.title: Dreams on canvas
intro.text: André Breton's 1924 manifesto: free the unconscious mind. Freud's ideas were everywhere.

intro.title: Two routes
intro.text: Precise dream scenes (Dalí, Magritte) or letting the hand wander freely (Miró, Ernst).

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Melting, floating or misplaced objects, eerie empty spaces, visual puns.

questions.q: Who wrote the Surrealist Manifesto in 1924?
questions.explain: A poet who had trained in medicine.

questions.q: Surrealism explores…
questions.explain: Inspired by Freud.

questions.q: The melting clocks painting is by…
questions.explain: The Persistence of Memory, 1931, at MoMA.

questions.q: Which is most Surrealist?
questions.explain: Dream logic, painted realistically.

questions.q: 'Ceci n'est pas une pipe' is written under a painting by…
questions.explain: The Treachery of Images, 1929.

questions.q: What's on top of Dalí's telephone at Tate?
questions.explain: Lobster Telephone, 1936, made for the collector Edward James.

questions.q: Dalí showed Metamorphosis of Narcissus to which visitor in London in 1938?
questions.explain: Freud had just fled Vienna.

intro.title: New York takes over
intro.text: After the Second World War, the centre of the art world moved from Paris to New York.

intro.title: Action painting
intro.text: Pollock laid canvas on the floor and dripped paint: the gesture is the subject.

intro.title: Colour field
intro.text: Rothko made huge glowing blocks of colour to swallow the viewer. Tate has a whole Rothko Room.

questions.q: Abstract Expressionism was centred in…
questions.explain: Pollock, Rothko, de Kooning, Krasner.

questions.q: Pollock's dripping technique is called…
questions.explain: The critic Harold Rosenberg's term, 1952.

questions.q: Rothko's paintings are…
questions.explain: Meant to be seen up close, in dim light.

questions.q: Rothko's Seagram murals were first meant for…
questions.explain: The Four Seasons in New York. He pulled out and later gave nine to Tate.

questions.q: When did Rothko's murals arrive at Tate?
questions.explain: They arrived on 25 February 1970, the day he was found dead.

intro.title: Born in Britain
intro.text: London's Independent Group got there first. Richard Hamilton's 1956 collage is often called the first Pop artwork.

intro.title: Then America
intro.text: Warhol's soup cans and Marilyns, Lichtenstein's comic-strip panels with Ben-Day dots.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Adverts, celebrities, comics, packaging. Flat bright colour, repetition, screenprinting.

questions.q: Pop Art took its imagery from…
questions.explain: Popular culture.

questions.q: Who made Campbell's Soup Cans?
questions.explain: 32 canvases, 1962. At MoMA.

questions.q: Lichtenstein copied printing dots from comics. They're called…
questions.explain: After the illustrator Benjamin Day.

questions.q: Warhol's favourite technique for repeating images was…
questions.explain: Fast, mechanical, endlessly repeatable.

questions.q: Whaam! (Tate) is based on…
questions.explain: A 1962 panel from All-American Men of War.

questions.q: Where was David Hockney born?
questions.explain: In 1937. He moved to LA in the 1960s.

questions.q: Marilyn Diptych was made…
questions.explain: In 1962. Colour on the left, fading black and white on the right.

intro.title: A British century
intro.text: Not one movement but a strong line: Spencer, Nash, Lowry, Moore, Hepworth, Bacon, Freud, Riley, Rego.

intro.title: Carving
intro.text: Henry Moore and Barbara Hepworth made British sculpture world-famous.

intro.title: School of London
intro.text: Bacon and Freud, friends and rivals, painted the body with raw intensity.

questions.q: Which sculptor lived and worked in St Ives, Cornwall?
questions.explain: Her studio and garden there are run by Tate.

questions.q: L.S. Lowry painted the industrial streets of…
questions.explain: Famous for crowds of 'matchstick' figures.

questions.q: Bridget Riley's black-and-white paintings belong to…
questions.explain: Optical art: patterns that seem to move.

questions.q: Francis Bacon's figures are usually…
questions.explain: Raw and unsettling.

questions.q: Stanley Spencer set The Resurrection in…
questions.explain: The dead rise from Cookham churchyard, Berkshire.

questions.q: Totes Meer (Dead Sea) by Paul Nash shows…
questions.explain: A sea of broken planes, painted in 1940–41.

questions.q: Paula Rego grew up in…
questions.explain: Born in Lisbon, she settled in London.

intro.title: Freeze, 1988
intro.text: Student Damien Hirst organised a show in an empty Docklands building. It launched a generation.

intro.title: The patron
intro.text: Adman Charles Saatchi bought heavily. His 'Sensation' show at the Royal Academy (1997) caused uproar.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Shock, everyday materials, death, confession: sharks in formaldehyde, unmade beds, casts of empty spaces.

questions.q: Which show launched the YBAs in 1988?
questions.explain: Organised by Hirst. Frieze, the fair, came later (2003).

questions.q: Who was the YBAs' big collector?
questions.explain: His 'Sensation' show went to the RA in 1997.

questions.q: YBA art often used…
questions.explain: Animals, beds, medicine cabinets.

questions.q: My Bed is a work by…
questions.explain: Shown at the Turner Prize in 1999.

questions.q: Pharmacy (Tate) was also the name of Hirst's…
questions.explain: A real restaurant, opened 1997.

intro.title: In the news
intro.text: Tate Britain's 'Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury' runs 12 November 2026 to 11 April 2027.

intro.title: The Bloomsbury Group
intro.text: Writers, painters and thinkers around Bloomsbury, London: Virginia Woolf (Vanessa's sister), Roger Fry, Maynard Keynes.

intro.title: Charleston
intro.text: From 1916 Bell and Grant lived at Charleston farmhouse in Sussex and painted every surface, walls and furniture included.

questions.q: Vanessa Bell's sister was…
questions.explain: The novelist.

questions.q: The Bloomsbury Group is named after…
questions.explain: Where many of them lived, around Gordon Square.

questions.q: Bell and Grant's bold colour came from seeing…
questions.explain: Roger Fry's 1910 and 1912 London shows changed their painting.

questions.q: Bloomsbury artists also designed…
questions.explain: Through Roger Fry's Omega Workshops.

questions.q: Bell and Grant's painted home in Sussex is…
questions.explain: Now open to visitors.

questions.q: Roger Fry's design company (1913) was the…
questions.explain: In Fitzroy Square. (The Hogarth Press was the Woolfs' publishing house.)

questions.q: Studland Beach (Tate) was painted by…
questions.explain: In 1912, simplifying figures into blocks of colour.

intro.title: In the news
intro.text: 'Peggy Guggenheim in London: The Making of a Collector' at the Royal Academy, 21 November 2026 to 14 March 2027.

intro.title: Cork Street
intro.text: Her first gallery, Guggenheim Jeune, ran at 30 Cork Street, London, 1938–39. It gave Kandinsky his first UK solo show.

intro.title: New York to Venice
intro.text: Her New York gallery championed a young Jackson Pollock. She ended up in a Venetian palazzo, now her museum.

questions.q: Peggy Guggenheim was famous as a…
questions.explain: One of the 20th century's great collectors.

questions.q: Her London gallery was called…
questions.explain: A pun on the Paris gallery Bernheim-Jeune.

questions.q: Her collection is strongest in…
questions.explain: She was briefly married to the Surrealist Max Ernst.

questions.q: Which young American did she champion in New York?
questions.explain: She gave him a contract and his first solo show (1943).

questions.q: Where is her collection now?
questions.explain: Palazzo Venier dei Leoni, on the Grand Canal.

intro.title: Sugar money
intro.text: Sugar refiner Henry Tate funded the first gallery at Millbank, opened 1897. Now Tate Britain.

intro.title: Four Tates
intro.text: Tate Britain and Tate Modern in London, plus Tate Liverpool and Tate St Ives.

intro.title: Turner Prize
intro.text: Set up in 1984, named after J.M.W. Turner, who left his work to the nation.

questions.q: Tate Modern is in a former…
questions.explain: Bankside Power Station, converted by Herzog & de Meuron, opened 2000.

questions.q: Henry Tate made his fortune from…
questions.explain: Tate & Lyle descends from his company.

questions.q: Which Tate shows British art from 1500 to now?
questions.explain: At Millbank, by the Thames.

questions.q: The Turner Prize began in…
questions.explain: Malcolm Morley was the first winner.

questions.q: Tate Britain's Clore Gallery holds…
questions.explain: Turner left around 300 oils and thousands of drawings to the nation.

intro.title: Founded 1824
intro.text: It began with 38 paintings bought from the banker John Julius Angerstein, and moved to Trafalgar Square in 1838.

intro.title: Free for all
intro.text: Western European painting from about 1250 to 1900, free to enter.

intro.title: Star pictures
intro.text: The Arnolfini Portrait, The Ambassadors, The Hay Wain, The Fighting Temeraire, Sunflowers.

questions.q: The National Gallery is on…
questions.explain: Since 1838.

questions.q: The National Gallery was founded in…
questions.explain: The British Museum is older (1753).

questions.q: The National Gallery's collection stops at about…
questions.explain: Later art is mostly at Tate.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT at the National Gallery?
questions.explain: Millais' Ophelia is at Tate Britain.

questions.q: The founding collection came from which banker?
questions.explain: 38 paintings bought by Parliament.

intro.title: Run by artists
intro.text: Founded by George III in 1768. Elected artists put 'RA' after their names.

intro.title: Summer Exhibition
intro.text: Every year since 1769: the world's oldest open-submission show. Anyone can enter.

intro.title: On now
intro.text: Painting the French Riviera, and from 21 November, Peggy Guggenheim in London.

questions.q: The Royal Academy is on…
questions.explain: Burlington House.

questions.q: Who founded the Royal Academy in 1768?
questions.explain: Reynolds was its first President.

questions.q: What's special about the Summer Exhibition?
questions.explain: Held every year since 1769.

questions.q: Which controversial YBA show did the RA host in 1997?
questions.explain: Charles Saatchi's collection.

intro.title: The big two
intro.text: Sotheby's (founded 1744) and Christie's (1766), both in London. Phillips is third.

intro.title: How a sale works
intro.text: Each lot has an estimate. The hammer price is the winning bid; the buyer then pays a premium on top.

intro.title: Records
intro.text: Salvator Mundi made $450.3m in 2017. Klimt's Lederer portrait made $236.4m in 2025.

questions.q: Which auction house is older?
questions.explain: Sotheby's, 1744. Christie's followed in 1766.

questions.q: The most expensive painting ever sold at auction is…
questions.explain: $450.3m, Christie's New York, 2017.

questions.q: The extra fee a buyer pays on top of the hammer price is the…
questions.explain: A percentage of the hammer price.

questions.q: The secret minimum price a seller will accept is the…
questions.explain: If bidding falls short, the lot is 'bought in'.

questions.q: A 'guarantee' at auction means…
options: The seller is promised a minimum price
questions.explain: Houses offer it to win big consignments.

questions.q: Interchange by de Kooning reportedly sold privately in 2015 for about…
questions.explain: One of the highest prices ever paid for a painting.

intro.title: Shopping malls for art
intro.text: Hundreds of galleries rent booths for a few days. Much of the year's selling happens here.

intro.title: Art Basel
intro.text: Founded in Basel in 1970. Now also Miami Beach, Hong Kong and Paris (in the Grand Palais).

intro.title: Frieze
intro.text: Frieze London launched in Regent's Park in 2003, with Frieze Masters for older art.

questions.q: Art Basel was founded in…
questions.explain: By Basel gallerists including Ernst Beyeler.

questions.q: Frieze London takes place in…
questions.explain: Every October.

questions.q: At an art fair, who sells the art?
questions.explain: Each gallery rents a booth.

questions.q: Where is Art Basel Paris held?
questions.explain: The restored Grand Palais.
